# **Descriptions of number systems**

## **Kunama (Tucker & Bryan 1966\)**

Personal pronouns have a three-way number distinction: singular, dual, and plural (see Table 1).

Table 1\. Personal pronouns in Kunama

|  | SG | DU | PL |
| :---- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| 1 | *a'ba* | EXCL. *'amme, aame*, INCL. *'kimme, kiime* | EXCL. *'ame*, INCL. *'kime* |
| 2 | *e'na* | *'emme, eeme* | *'eme* |
| 3 | *u'nu* | *'imme, iime* | *'ime* |

Possessive suffixes distinguish the number of the possessor only by stress, with plural suffix being stressed and singular being unstressed (*'mas-an-a* ‘my spear’, *mas-'an-a* ‘our spear’).  
Nouns are obligatorily marked in the singular (-*a*) and the plural (-*e*). Adjectives have the same suffixes (-*a* and \-*e*) when they agree with the head noun. Some interrogative and demonstrative pronouns also appear to take these suffixes.  
“Class I” verbs (mostly intransitive) are indexed with suffixes that distinguish singular and plural number of the subject (S/A), while “class II” verbs (mostly transitive) are indexed with prefixes that distinguish singular, dual, and plural number of the subject. If the subject is 2nd or 3rd person, “class II” verbs may attach 1st or 2nd person object (P) prefixes in place of subject prefixes (hierarchical system?).  
Some “class II” verbs have stem alternation for number of the subject distinguishing singular, dual, and plural (e.g., SG[^1] *i* — DU *imi* — PL *ili* ‘arrive’). Other verbs have an added element *\-l-* or *\-n-* in the plural form (SG *egi* — PL *ilagi* ‘run’; SG *ena* — PL *enana* ‘sing’). “Class II” verbs indicate plural objects by *(i)n(a)-* or partial reduplication for verbs with a double consonant (*na-ite-ke* ‘I found (one)’, *na-n-ite-ke* ‘I found (many)’; *illi-ke* ‘he bound ( one)’, *ilili-ke* ‘he bound (many)’).

Summary on VDU: “Class I” verbs index singular and plural S/A participants cumulatively with person, while “Class II” verbs distinguish singular, dual, and plural S/A participants cumulatively with person. Some “Class II” verbs additionally show stem alternation conditioned by S/A number (singular, dual, and plural), while other verbs form plural stems by means of the added elements *\-l-* or \-*n*\-. Plural P participants may be marked by the prefix *(i)n(a)-* or by partial reduplication. Outside the verbal domain, personal pronouns distinguish singular, dual, and plural forms, while possessive suffixes, nouns and agreeing adjectives distinguish singular and plural forms.

## **Ama (Stevenson 1938\)**

It is characteristic of the Nyimang group that number is shown in the verb rather than in the noun (Tucker & Bryan 1966: 246). A few human nouns have a separate plural stem. Reduplication of the first syllable of nouns and some adjectives denotes distributivity.   
Personal pronouns distinguish singular and plural forms cumulatively with person and case.  Possessive pronouns exhibit the same distinctions and are fused with the nominal root. The interrogative pronoun ‘who’ has singular and plural, the latter is formed with the suffix \-*ŋi* which also occurs on some plural noun forms in other Nyimang languages (Tucker & Bryan 1966: 246).  
Many verbs mark participant number by means of suffixes (see Table 2). Suffix *\-(i)n* denotes dual of S/P/A participant (i.e. if any of the participants is dual, this suffix is used), *\-di* denotes plural of S/P (and maybe A) participant. These suffixes are presented in the table below, suffixes in brackets are used for intransitive verbs, but reported in (Tucker & Bryan 1966: 250\) for transitive verbs as well. Dual forms are gradually going out of use, singular or plural may be used instead (e.g. *aŋi a morde kwa* (instead of *kwen*) ‘I am going with the horse.’). 

Table 2\. Ama number suffixes on verbs

| S(A)/P      | SG (or no P) | DU | PL |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| SG | *—* | *\-in* | *\-di* |
| DU | *(-in)* | *\-in* | *\-d-in* |
| PL | *(-di)* | *\-in* | *\-di* |

Summary on VDU: There are productive dual and plural suffixes on verbs, they may denote number of S/A?/P participants. However, dual forms are gradually going out of use, singular or plural may be used instead. Only a few nouns distinguish number (singular and plural), pronouns distinguish singular and plural.

## **Chipewyan (Cook 2004\)**

Independent personal pronouns have a common form for first and second person plural. Possessive prefixes distinguish the following forms: 1 — *se*\-; 2 — *ke*\-; 3 — *be*\-; (11)/12/22 — *nuhe*\-; 33 *hube-/behe*\-; 4 — *ye*\-. “Dual” forms of these prefixes may be interpreted as plural depending on the context (they are called ‘duoplural’).  
Subject prefixes distinguish singular and plural for first, second, and third person. Object prefixes have a common form for first and second person plural (‘duoplural’), there is no paradigmatic number contrast for third person. Prefix *he*\- optionally marks plural third person subject (1). Prefix *dá-* is an optional derivational marker that encodes distributive plurality of S/A/P, or sometimes other lexicalized meanings, it is usually combined with the plural marker.

(1)	a.	*tsąba hułtá* ‘he is counting money’  
b.	*tsąba **he**hułtá* ‘they (two) are counting money’  
c.	*tsąba **dáhe**hułtá / **dá**hułtá* ‘all of them are counting money’

There are some verbs that have stem alternation to indicate the number of the S (and ?) participant: singular, dual, and plural (SG \-*ghał* — DU \-*ʔás* — PL \-*dë́ł* ‘walk’), or non-plural and plural \[3+\] (NPL \-*tį* — PL\[3+\] \-*yi* ‘eat’), or singular and plural (SG *l-goł —* PL  \-*ʔás* ‘crawl’).

Summary on VDU: Some verbs have number-conditioned stem alternation, distinguishing singular/dual/plural, non-plural/plural \[3+\]  or singular/plural of S/? participant. Verbs separately index singular and plural S/A and P participants, although with some syncretism. Distributive plurality may additionally be expressed by the derivational prefix *dá-*. Independent pronouns and possessive prefixes distinguish only singular and plural.

## **Navajo (Young & Morgan 1987\)**

Kinship terms and some human nouns can be pluralized by adding a suffix \-*ké,* or in a few instances suffix *\-óó / \- yóó* (SG *’ashkii* — PL *’ashii**ké*** ‘boy(s)’). Nouns ‘person, tribe, nation’ and ‘adult male’ have an irregular plural.   
Personal pronouns distinguish singular and plural for first and second person. Pronouns may also take the distributive plural prefix *da*\- (\>2), either in addition to plural marking or on singular forms when no dedicated plural form is available.  
Subject prefixes distinguish singular and plural number in the first and second person. Some verbs have different stems for singular, dual, and plural \[3+\] reference of S/? participant (SG *yá* — DU ‘*áázh* — PL\[3+\] *kai* ‘go’). The plural \[3+\] form is usually used with collective reference (distributive plurality is expressed separately). The choice of the verbal stem can mismatch syntactic agreement (2).

(2)	*shí	ashkii	bi-ł		yi-sh-ʼash*  
I	boy	him-with	prog-1sg-walk.du  
‘I'm walking with the boy.’ (Jeanne, Hale & Pranka 1984 cited in Durie 1986: 358\)

Distributive prefix *da*\- may combine with any word class to indicate distributive plurality. In the verb, it is a III position prefix that can pluralize S/A/P participants (*tsin bąąh ha**da**sii’na’* ‘we (3+ each) climbed the tree’). 

Summary on VDU: Some verbs have number-conditioned stem alternation distinguishing singular, dual, and plural \[3+\] stems of S/? participant. Verbs index singular and plural S/A participants cumulatively with person. The choice of the verbal stem can show a mismatch with indexing. Distributive prefix *da*\- may combine with verbs and other word classes and, in the verb, can pluralize S, A, or P participants. Outside the verbal domain, personal pronouns and nouns distinguish singular and plural but not dual.

## **North Slavey (Rice 1989\)**

Personal pronouns have a common plural form for the first and second person, and a distinct form for the third person. Possessive pronouns distinguish four persons and also have a common plural form for the first and second person.  
Optional plural suffix \-*ke* may occur on some nouns (humans and dogs) and demonstratives. When the subject of a sentence is marked for plurality by the suffix \-*ke*, it is not necessary to use the human plural number prefix *ke*\- in the verb (3).

(3)	a.	*John	be-ya-**ke**	ʔeyá	yįlé*  
  		John	3-son-pl	sick	3.be.pst  
		‘John’s sons were sick’  
	b. 	*John beya ʔeyá **ke**yįlé*    
		‘John’s sons were sick’  
	c.	 *John beyake ʔeyá **ke**yįlé *   
		‘John’s sons were sick’.

Prefix *ke*\- marks human plural subject in the third person, while *ts'e*\- marks unspecified human subject. Subject person-number prefixes distinguish singular and plural for first and second person (the third person is unmarked). However, first person plural in Bearlake dialect is generally restricted to dual. Object prefixes distinguish first person singular and second person singular, with a common plural form, while for the third person the choice of the prefix also depends on the subject (there is also a fourth person object prefix, which doesn’t have number distinction).   
Some verbs also require number prefixes for dual (*łéh*\-) and plural (*go*\-); e.g. SG *detla* ‘s/he starts out’ — DU *łekedetla* ‘they two start out’ — PL *gokedéhwe* ‘they (plural) started out’. In most examples, these prefixes indicate the number of S participants in movement verbs, however, it is mentioned that they may also indicate the number of the P participant (p. 431).  
Some verbs have different stems conditioned by the number of the S participant, and possibly also the P participant: singular/dual/plural (SG *whida* — DU *whíkee* — PL *ts’edéhkw’i* ‘be seated’), or singular/plural (SG *shǫtį* — PL *shukiya* ‘sleep’), or non-plural/plural \[3+\]. “Generally, in Slave, it is important that the verb stem agree in number with the overt subject marker. Combining a plural subject marker with a singular stem is impossible in Slave for first and second person subjects (Keren Rice, p.c.).” (Veselinova 2013\) However, as reported in (Corbett 2010: 249), “dual is not strictly for two but may be used for a small number (Keren Rice, personal communication)”.  
The prefix *yá*\- can indicate distributive plurality of S/P participant (*kade* ‘they (PL) are walking’ — ***yá**kade* ‘they (PL) are each walking’; *ts’éré réta* ‘s/he rolled up the blanket’ — *ts’éré **yá**nįta* ‘s/he rolled up each blanket, one blanket after another’), including spatial distributivity (*nágedéhya* ‘they are standing’ — *ná**á**gedéhya* ‘they are standing here and there’), and intraoccasional plurality (*déta* ‘it kicked’ — ***yá**dįta* ‘it kicked many times’).

Summary on VDU: Some verbs have number-conditioned stem alternation distinguishing singular/dual/plural, singular/plural, or non-plural/plural \[3+\] forms of S and possibly P participants. Some verbs also take number prefixes for dual and plural, mostly indicating the number of S participants in movement verbs, but also reported for P participants. Verbs separately index singular and plural S/A and P participants cumulatively with person. A plural subject marker cannot combine with a singular stem for first and second person subjects, while third person plural marking is optional. Dual may be used for a small number rather than strictly for two. The prefix *yá*\- can indicate distributive plurality of S/P or intraoccasional plurality. (Pro)nominal number may distinguish singular and plural, but not dual.

## **Sarsi (Cook 1984\)**

Personal pronouns have person-number stems distinguishing singular and plural. Demonstratives may also show number-conditioned stem alternation.  
Relativizing suffixes encode contrasts in number and gender: \-*ná* is used for human or plural referents (for dual in complementizers, with plural marked by *\-ná-ìná*), while \-*í* is used for non-human or singular referents. The latter may also function as an unmarked option when gender and number are predictable from context.  
A small class of nouns, mostly kinship terms and terms referring to a reciprocal relationship that is marked by a special prefix, may attach plural/collective suffix \-*ká* (SG *is-ts’òyà* — NSG *ís-ts’òyà-ká* ‘wife’). The same suffix may be copied onto a dependent numeral or relative clause. Suffix \-*yìná* may attach to kinship terms, personal names, and nouns after a demonstrative to indicate collective or associative plurality, or sometimes deference (*ìlk’ōōts’í yìná* ‘Bull-Head and his companion’). There are also several irregular residual plural forms (SG *ts’ìkà* — NSG *ts’ìkùwá* ‘young woman’).  
Separate prefixes index 1st and 2nd person for subject and object distinguishing singular and plural. Prefix *gi*\- may optionally indicate 3rd person plural of either subject or object.    
A small set of verbs has different stems for non-plural and plural \[3+\] of S/P (*īdìs**gàh*** ‘I’ll go off with a pack’; *īdāà**gàh*** ‘We (du) will go off with a pack’ ; *īdāàdàt* ‘We (pl) will go off with a pack’), some verbs form plural \[3+\] with an optional prefix *da*\-. For classificatory verbs, all distinctions are neutralized in the plural, apart from animacy. An even smaller set of intransitive verbs exhibit a three-way contrast: singular, dual, and plural (*dì**yáh*** ‘He starts to walk.’ — *gídì**t’òs*** ‘They (two) start to walk.’ — *gídí**dàł*** ‘They (three or more) start to walk.’). Sometimes, plural stems may occur with singular subject (but not with a dual) to indicate an accompanied action (*tīnā gūk’àγìh γīdìł-lā* ‘Following the tracks she was walking with it (in company with others).’).

Summary on VDU: A small set of intransitive verbs has number-conditioned stem alternation distinguishing singular, dual, and plural S participants. Some verbs distinguish non-plural and plural \[3+\] stems for S/P participants. plural stems may sometimes occur with a singular subject to indicate accompanied action, but not with a dual subject. Classificatory verbs neutralize most distinctions in the plural apart from animacy. Verbs separately index S/A and P distinguishing first and second person singular and plural participants, while *gi*\- may optionally indicate third person plural S/A/P. (Pro)nominal number may distinguish singular and plural but not dual.

## **Notes on Sarsi and other Athapaskan (Cook 1974\)**

Many Athapaskan languages show number-conditioned stem alternation for S/P participants (Sarsi, Navajo, Chipewyan, Kaska, Tahltan). A closer look at the verb ‘arrive’ in Sarsi (which was describe to have three-way number system) shows that in continuative singular stem is used instead of dual. A similar development is observed in Navaho by Hoijer who points out that the singular stem *yá* ‘arrive’ may be used in singular or plural. So the author suggests that this stem originated as singular and developed into non-plural. Non-plural stems either have a corresponding plural \[3+\] stem or may attach prefix *da*\- (which may also occur with plural \[3+\] stems). A similar prefix is observed in other Athapaskan languages, and is described as a distributive prefix or plural formed by incorporation of the particle da. In Sarsi, this prefix is not obligatory, so the stems may be both non-plural and plural \[3+\] without it. The author suggests the following development of verbal number system in Sarsi:

(I) singular/dual/plural \[3+\] → (II) non-plural/plural \[3+\] → (III) non-plural/plural \[3+\] with *da*\- → (IV) unrestricted

First lost are dual stems as the type II system became predominant, next lost are plural \[3+\] stems as they are replaced by stems with the more productive prefix *da*\-, and finally, the prefix *da*\- has begun to lose its grammatical function.

## **Kaska (Moore 2002\)**

Independent personal pronouns have person-number stems distinguishing singular and plural. Possessive prefixes and indexes on verbs have a similar system. Subject prefixes (in position 2 and 7\) distinguish singular and plural number cumulative with person. Sets of direct object prefixes, oblique object pronouns used with postpositions and possessive prefixes on nouns are almost identical, and they also distinguish singular and plural number cumulative with person.  
The prefix *łe*\- is used to form dual S of the verb ‘sit’. The prefixes *ne-* and *ye-* are used to indicate plural \[3+\] subjects (*nédzéhtʼés* ‘we (plural) are cooking’ — *dzehtʼés* ‘we both are cooking’), as well as distributive (and intraoccasional?).  
Some verbs have distinct dual and plural stems (‘walk around’, ‘sit’, ‘go along’). “Dual and plural verb forms may be used to indicate the social solidarity of some characters, as opposed to the social isolation of characters referred to with singular verb forms”.   
Summary on VDU: Prefixes *ne-/ye-* indicates plural \[3+\] S/A participants and may additionally express distributive (and possibly intraoccasional) meanings. When plural person-number prefixes occur without *ne-/ye*\-, the verb may be interpreted as dual. Some verbs have distinct stems for dual and plural S (?) participants, including ‘walk around’, ‘sit’, and ‘go along’. Prefix *łe-* is used to form dual subject forms of the verb ‘sit’. Dual and plural verbal forms may also indicate social solidarity between participants, contrasting with the social isolation associated with singular forms. (Pro)nominal number distinguishes singular and plural but not dual. 

## **Tahltan (Alderete & Blenkiron 2014\)**

Subject prefixes on verbs distinguish singular and plural for first and second person (third person is unmarked). Object prefixes have a common plural form for first and second person, and a distinct form for third person  plural. Oblique object pronouns and possessive prefixes are almost identical and distinguish singular and plural number cumulatively with person.  
Prefix *da*\- “can refer to action done separately on plural objects or collectively on plural subjects”.  
Some verbs have different stems distinguishing singular, dual, and plural number of the S (?) participant (‘sit’, ‘go’, ‘come’; Nater 2006: 55; Cook 1973: 102).  
Summary on VDU: Some verbs have distinct singular, dual, and plural stems indicating the number of the S participant, including ‘sit’, ‘go’, and ‘come’. In addition, the prefix *da*\- may indicate actions performed separately on plural objects or collectively by plural subjects. Pronominal number distinguishes singular and plural but not dual.

## **Karuk (Bright 1957\)**

Plural suffix \-*sa(s)* (and its allomorphs) may optionally occur on some human nouns and independent adjectives (e.g., *ʔávansa* ‘man’ — *ʔávan-asa* ‘men’; *kêč* ‘big’ — *kêč-asa* ‘big ones’).  
All verbs have a slot for one indexing morpheme that indicates person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural) of both subject and object, as well as mood (indicative or imperative).  
Suffix \-*na* (and its allomorphs) may optionally mark plural subjects for verbs of the “personal class” and plural objects for verbs of the “transpersonal class” (SG *čúphi —* PL *čúphi-na ‘talk’)*. It usually refers to human participants. The cluster of suffixes *\-ar-a-hi* can express collective subject plural (*imkánva* ‘to gather (food)’ —  *imkanvárahi* ‘to gather food collectively’).  
Suffix \-*va* indicates participant (*θivrúhtih* ‘(one object) to be floating’ — *θivrúhtih-va* ‘(several objects) to be floating’) or spatial (*vúrunih* ‘to flow down (in a single stream)’ — *vurúnih-va* ‘to flow down (in several streams)’) distributive, as well as intraoccasional (*yuh* ‘to spit’ — *yúh-va* ‘to vomit’) and interoccasional plurality or habitual (?). For some verbs, \-*va* has a lexicalized meaning.  
For several verbs, initial elements *ik*\- and *iθ-* may correspond to singular and dual subject respectively (SG *ikpuh* — DU *iθpuh* ‘to swim’*)*.  
Several verbs have different stems for singular, dual, and plural subjects (SG *ikri* — DU *ʔina —* PL *ʔarahitih* ‘to live, sit’*)*. Several other verbs have different stems for singular and plural inanimate objects (*paθ-*‘to throw (one thing)’ *— ixya* ‘to throw (two or more things)’. Where such stem alternations exist, the corresponding stem is obligatory.   
Partial reduplication of the verb indicates inraoccasional plurality (*tásir̄* ‘to brush (once)’ — *tasín-sir̄* ‘to brush repeatedly’).

Summary on VDU: Several verbs have obligatory number-conditioned stem alternation distinguishing singular, dual, and plural S participants. For several verbs, the initial elements *ik-* and *iθ-* may correspond to singular and dual S participants, respectively. Several other verbs have different stems for singular and plural inanimate P participants. The optional suffix *\-na* marks plural S participants with verbs of the “personal class” and plural P participants with verbs of the “transpersonal class”, usually with human referents. Verbs index singular and plural S/A+P participants cumulatively with person. Additionally, collective subject plurality may be expressed by *\-ar-a-hi*, while event number may be expressed by *\-va* or partial verbal reduplication. Outside the verbal domain, some human nouns and independent adjectives may optionally distinguish plural but not dual. 

## **Western Keres (Lachler 2005\)**

Number is usually not marked on the noun; however, there are two optional ways to express it: collective suffix \-*ty'itra* (*ch'ayaanyi* ‘shaman’ — *ch'ayaanyity'itra* ‘(group of) shamans’) and plural \-*dyeimishe* (which is composed of a verbalizing suffix \-*dyei* ‘have several of something’ and the general nominalizing suffix \-*Cishe*). The latter is attested only with possessed nouns.   
Possessive prefixes distinguish singular, dual, and plural cumulatively with person. Corresponding elements *\-a-, \-a’a-,* and *\-aya-* can be identified, while the beginning element is different depending on the person and singular and dual / plural number.  
In the majority of verbs, number suffixes (dual \-*nɨ* and plural \-*na,* see 4\) encode number of the subject for transitive, reflexive, reciprocal, benefactive, and some intransitive verb themes (S/A participants). The plural suffix is obligatory with passive themes. Stem alternation encodes singular, dual, or plural number for the object of transitive (e.g., SG *\-ukacha* — DU *\-u'ukacha* — PL *\-uwakacha* ‘see something’) and benefactive themes and for the subject of passive and some intransitive themes (S/P participants). However, some transitive verbs do not obligatorily specify the number of their object, especially when it is inanimate. These alternations may also be analyzed as semi-regular and highly lexicalized fusion with number prefixes, but this analysis is not synchronically obvious. 

(4)	a.	*g-uwakacha*   
3ACT:DIR-see.sth.PL   
‘he saw them PL ’  
b.	*g-uwakacha-nɨ*   
3ACT:DlR-see.sth.PL-DL   
‘they DL saw them PL ’  
c.	*g-uwakacha-na*   
3ACT:DlR-see.sth.PL-PL   
‘they PL saw them PL ’

A smaller number of verbs (“suffixing verbs”) show a different pattern of inflection, taking suffixes that cumulatively express person, role, mood, polarity, and number (singular, dual, and plural), which were grammaticalized from auxiliary verbs. Some of these verbs also have reduplicated forms which express plurality of the subject or intraoccasional plurality. 

Summary on VDU: In the majority of verbs, the suffix \-*nɨ* marks dual S/A participants, while \-*na* marks plural S/A participants; the plural suffix is obligatory with passive themes. Stem alternation marks singular, dual, and plural number of P participants in transitive and benefactive themes, and of S participants in passive and some intransitive themes. Some transitive verbs do not obligatorily specify the number of their P participant, especially when it is inanimate. A smaller class of “suffixing verbs” takes suffixes cumulatively expressing person, role, mood, polarity, and singular, dual, or plural number. Some of these verbs also have reduplicated forms expressing plurality of the subject or intraoccasional plurality. Outside the verbal domain, possessive prefixes distinguish singular, dual, and plural possessors, while nominal number is usually unmarked, although collective and plural markers may occur optionally.

## **Notes on Muskogean (Booker 1978\)**

Number marking originated in intransitive verbs expressing some kind of location, either static or moving. It then spread to locative transitives, and sporadically to intransitives outside the locative semantic domain.  
Two PM number markers are reconstructed: a dualizer \**ho* and a pluralizer \**či*. The morphemes were eventually bleached of their meaning and alternative methods arose to preserve the number distinctions. Reflexes of \**ho* may appear in dual and plural \[2+\] in Creek, and only in plural \[2+\] in Choctaw, Koasati, and Mikasuki. Reflexes of  \**či* may appear in plural \[3+\] and plural \[2+\] in Creek, in plural \[3+\] in Mikasuki, in dual in Koasati, in dual and plural \[2+\] in Choctaw. In Choctaw, there are synonymous doublets of plural \[2+\] forms for some verbs — with \**ho* or with \**či.*

## **Choctaw (Broadwell 2006\)**

First person pronouns distinguish singular, paucal, and plural, while second person pronouns distinguish singular and plural (there are no distinct third person pronouns). Possessive pronouns used in a predicative context also distinguish singular, paucal, and plural for the first person, and singular and plural for the second person, while the third person does not distinguish number.  
Like personal pronouns, verbal indexes distinguish singular, paucal, and plural in the first person, and singular and plural in the second person. There are three sets of prefixes (and one suffix for 1sg in set I): for subject, direct object and indirect object (source or goal). However, in set I paucal and plural synchronically are not distinguished. In third person, the preverb *oklah=* (derived from the noun ‘people’) may be used to indicate a plural animate subject. The prefix *ho(o)- / (o)oh-* appears in the second person plural imperative.  
Some verbs show stem alternation for the number of the S/P participant, or the argument which bears the thematic role Theme. Some verbs (mostly verbs of motion and location) make a three-way distinction between singular, dual, and plural (SG *iyah* — DU *ittiyaachih* — PL *ilhkolih* ‘to go’), while others only distinguish singular and plural stems (SG *kobaffih* ‘to break \[one long object\]’ — PL *kobahlih* ‘to break (two or more long objects)’).   
There are some verbal suffixes listed as quantifiers. Suffix \-*bika* ‘both’ is a marker of duality, and requires that some dual argument be present in the sentence (5). Suffix \-*biika* indicates distributivity over S/P (?) participants (6) or space, as well as intraoccasional and interoccasional plurality. Suffix \-*tokla* used by some speakers marks a dual subject. It is sometimes used with the singular forms of suppletive verbs (7). The similarity of \-*tokla* to the numeral *tokloh* ‘two’ should be noted.

(5)	*Ii-hilha-bika-tok.*   
lPl-dance-both-PT   
‘We (two) danced.’   
(6)	*. . . okchaya-t	ik-may-ok-aachi-ka,	im-allosi-ya	isht-kampila-biika-ttook.*  
live-PART	N-be:PL-NEG-IRR-COMP	III-baby-AC	INSTR-throw:away-DISTR-DPAST   
‘They threw their children away so that they wouldn’t (have to) live. ’  
(7)	*Tamaaha’	iya-tokla-tok.*   
town		go:SG-DU-PT   
‘They (two) went to town.' 

Summary on VDU:  Several verbs have different stems that distinguish singular, dual, and plural number of S/P participants, while some other verbs have different stems only for singular and plural. Suffix  \-*bika* ‘both’ may indicate duality of some argument (S/A/P), and suffix \-*tokla* (derived from ‘two’) used by some speakers marks a dual subject and is sometimes used with the singular forms of suppletive verbs. These forms do not have a corresponding plural form, apart from distributive \-*biika.* There is no nominal number, and pronominal number and verbal indexing do not distinguish dual.

## **Creek (Martin 2011\)**

Most nouns lack plural forms; however, a few human nouns form plural with suffix \-*aki* or *\-ta:ki*. Suffix \-*âlki* (probably derived from the quantifier *alk*\- ‘every, each’) may indicate group plural, and it is commonly used with names of clans (*fóswa* ‘bird'  — *fosw-âlki* ‘Bird clan’). Nominalizations may be singular or plural because they retain this feature from the verb. A noun may also sometimes be interpreted as plural because the word modifying it is plural.  
Personal pronouns distinguish singular and plural in first and second person. Possessive prefixes distinguish singular and plural only in first person.   
Agent agreement suffixes distinguish singular and plural in first and second person. Patient agreement prefixes, as well as dative prefixes, distinguish singular and plural only in first person. Intransitive verbs may use agent or patient markers depending on the agentivity of the subject.  
Some common verbs show stem alternation to indicate plurality of the theme (S/P). Verbs referring to position or movement and several transitive verbs make a three-way distinction between singular, dual, and plural \[3+\]. Some other verbs distinguish singular and plural. Many dual and plural stems include an element \-*ho*\-, the basic meaning of \-*ho*\- is plural (two or more). When there is a special plural \[3+\] form, however, the form with \-*ho*\- is limited to dual. Some intransitive plural \[3+\] verb stems are formed by dropping the final *k* of the singular and adding an element \-*ic*\-.   
Reduplication may indicate that the theme is plural or distributed in location or time. It is most commonly found with stative verbs or adjectives (8). Reduplication is limited to intransitive verbs, but intransitive reduplicated verbs can be made transitive.

(8)	*am-istilipeyka	laslat-k-t	ô:-s*   
1S.DAT-shoe	black.RED-DUR-T	be.FGR-IND   
‘My shoes are black.’

Several verbs may replace their final consonant or consonants with \-*hl* in order to indicate distributive or intraoccasional plurality (*falap-itá* ‘to split (one)’ — *falahli:c-itá* ‘to split (two or more, or one in pieces)’; *(i)ti-pakoc-itá* ‘to fold once, double’ — *(i)ti-pakohleyc-itá* ‘to fold several times’).   
Suffix \-*ak*\- appears on verbs or adjectives to indicate a plural S/P if plurality is not specified otherwise (by person marking, suppletion, reduplication, or \-*hl*).  
Woven objects or objects made of cloth are treated as duals. With verbs showing a three-way distinction, the dual is used for one or two woven items, and the plural \[3+\] is used for three or more (9a–b). If a verb makes a two-way distinction, the plural is used for one or more. Items with many particles or strands (like sand, salt, or hair) and liquids are treated as plurals \[3+\] (9c).

(9)	a.	*káːpa-t	oh-homp-itá-n	oh-káːk-is*  
		coat-T	LOC-eat-INF-N	LOC-sit.DUFGR-IND  
‘A coat \[or two coats\] is \[sitting\] on the table.’  
	b.	*káːpa-t	oh-homp-itá-n	ohh-apôːk-is*  
		coat-T	LOC-eat-INF-N	LOC-sit.TPLFGR-IND  
‘Coats \[three or more\] are \[sitting\] on the table.’  
	c.	*okcánwa-t	oh-homp-itá-n	oh-lóːmh-is*  
		salt-T	LOC-eat-INF-N	LOC-lie.TPLFGR-IND  
‘There’s salt \[lying\] on the table.’

Summary on VDU: Several verbs (mostly position and movement verbs) have different stems that distinguish singular, dual, and plural \[3+\] number of S/P participants, some other verbs have different stems only for singular and plural. These alternations should be regarded as derivational, since nominalizations and transitivized verbs retain corresponding distinctions.  Many dual (if there is a dedicated plural \[3+\] form) and plural stems include an element \-*ho*\-. Woven objects or objects made of cloth are treated as duals, items with many particles or strands and liquids are treated as plural \[3+\]. There are other strategies for verbal plural forms, and pronominal number, nominal number, and indexing which do not distinguish dual.

## **Koasati (Kimball 1991\)**

Independent pronouns, as well as nominal possessive prefixes, distinguish singular and plural number for first and second person.   
Human nouns may optionally indicate plurality with the suffix \-*ha*. Nouns derived either historically or synchronically with the diminutive suffix \-*(o)si*, form paucal (more than two but less than five or six) with the suffix \-*ki*, and multiple plural with the combination of \-*ki* and \-*ha*. Mass nouns require a plural verb form.  
Verbs show person and number of the subject, direct object, and indirect object (dative / benefactive) in different slots through suffixes or prefixes (depending on the conjugation class and values of the categories), distinguishing singular and plural number for first and second person.   
There are several strategies to express the number of S/P participants. Some verbs may show ‘formative replacement’ (stem alternation that was historically an alternation between singular and plural formatives) to express plural (?) S/P participant or intraoccasional plurality. Some other verbs have stem alternation distinguishing singular, dual, and plural (SG *á:ial* — DU *áswan* — PL *í:san* ‘to dwell’), or non-plural and plural \[3+\] (NPL *íllin* —  PL\[3+\] *hápkan* ‘to die’), or singular and plural (SG *í:sin* — PL *píhlin*) of S/P participant. Several verbs have the same root in singular and plural, but with some irregular extensions or deletions. Partial reduplication may indicate repeated action with active verbs and plurality of S with stative verbs (SG *aló:tkan* — PL *alotló:kan* ‘to be full’). Some other verbs form plural S/P forms by infixing *\-s-* before the ultimate syllable (SG *aká:non* — PL *akásnon* ‘to be hungry’).  
Suffix \-*ci* appears with several verbs. It marks third person dual in verbs that have a distinct plural \[3+\] stem (and a non-plural stem) and third person plural in those that do not, it may also occur as an additional plural marker for verbs that undergo formative replacement, and with some verbs, it may encode repeated or extended action (*páłłin* ‘to split up something’ — *pałłí:cin* ‘to splinter something’).  
Prefix *ho-/oh-* optionally marks S/A/P distributive, it also marks plural for adjectives that do not have a special form. It is also used to indicate that an actor in the verb phrase is indefinite and to derive the passive. Duplication of this prefix forms the “iterative” prefix *hoho*\- which indicates interoccasional plurality and occurs quite rarely (hoho-koybóhli-l ‘he stole from time to time’).   
Summary on VDU: Several verbs have different stems that distinguish singular, dual, and plural number of S/P participants. Most other verbs distinguish singular and plural of S/P, and some distinguish non-plural and plural \[3+\]. A rarely occurring suffix \-*ci* marks third person dual in verbs that have a distinct plural \[3+\] stem (and a non-plural stem) and third person plural in those that do not. (Pro)nominal number, as well as indexing on verbs, only distinguish singular and plural number. 

## **Mikasuki (Boynton 1982\)**

Personal pronouns, as well as inalienable possessive prefixes, show number distinction between singular and plural only in the first person.   
Nouns that are marked for inalienable possession may attach the plural suffix \-*ho*. As a prefix, *ho*\- may optionally mark plural on human nouns. \-*ho*\- is also optionally used as a verbal infix to indicate second or third person human plural of S, A, P, or R, or as a pronominal infix in second person plural. The “general plural suffix” \-*a:ł* optionally marks plural on nouns and may co-occur with *ho*\- to convey the meaning ‘all of the…’ (e.g., *ho-tayk-a:ł-ot* ‘(all of the) women’). It also functions as a nominalizer when attached to verbs (‘people/things who V’).  
Verbs have suffixes that index person (1st or 2nd) and number (singular or plural) of the agent and prefixes that index person (1st, 2nd, or 3rd) and number (singular or plural, only for the 1st person) of the patient.  
A number of common verbs (transitive, intransitive referring to action, or positional) have irregular stem alternation for the number of S, A, P, or R. For some verbs, irregular stem alternation may encode intraoccasional plurality along with or without participant plurality. Some verbs show a two-way distinction (singular and plural) and others show a three-way distinction (singular, dual, and plural \[3+\]). Adjectives, which behave like stative predicates, have only two numbers. There are verbs that follow some patterns in the formation of their stems. These patterns are the same for dual and plural \[2+\] stems, while the plural \[3+\] is formed from the dual. Cloth-like items take dual or plural stems, and liquids take plural or plural \[3+\] stems regardless of the number of items.

Summary on VDU: A number of common verbs have number-conditioned stem alternation for S/A/P/R participants. Some verbs distinguish singular and plural stems, while others distinguish singular, dual, and plural \[3+\] stems. For some verbs, stem alternation may also encode intraoccasional plurality, with or without participant plurality. Some verbs follow semi-regular patterns of stem formation, with the same patterns used for dual and plural stems, and the plural \[3+\] formed from the dual. Cloth-like items are treated as duals, while liquids are treated as plurals \[3+\]. Verbs also separately index singular and plural S/A and P participants cumulatively with person (but P distinguishes number only in the first person). Outside the verbal domain, personal pronouns and possessive prefixes distinguish singular and plural only in the first person; nominal plural may be marked, but no (pro)nominal dual is reported.

## **Wichita (Rood 1976\)**

There is no (pro)nominal number.   
On the verb, *hi’-* indicates plural subject, *\-‘ak* or *rV* – third person plural patient (S/P), *ra:k* — non–third person plural \[3+\] object (P), *hi’...’ak* — non–third person dual object (see Figure 1). For third person plural patient, the distribution of the two markers usually corresponds to the collective / non-collective distinction. Motion verbs add the preverb *uc*\- and the morpheme *wakhahr* to indicate collective. Some other verbs (‘break down’, ‘burn’, ‘cut off’, ‘eat’, ‘fall over’, ‘grind’, ‘kill’ ‘say’) have idiosyncratic forms to mark plural patient (?).   
A few active verbs (‘come’, ‘go by’, ‘sit’, ‘stand’, ‘sit down’, and their derivatives) also take the suffix \-*wa* which occurs with *hi’*\- to indicate dual subject. Several other verbs (‘be’, ‘go’) indicate dual by stem alternation.

Figure 1\.  
![][image1]

Summary on VDU: Number is expressed exclusively on the verb. A is marked for number if P is unmarked (singular). *hi’*\- marks plural A/S(?) participants. Several other markers are cumulative with person: \-*’ak* (distributive) and *rV* (collective) mark third person plural patients, *ra:k* marks non-third person plural \[3+\] objects, and *hi’…’ak* marks non-third person dual objects. A few active verbs distinguish dual S/A participants by means of the suffix \-*wa*, which cooccurs with the plural marker *hi’*\-, while several other verbs indicate dual through stem alternation. Certain motion verbs also have special collective forms, and some verbs exhibit idiosyncratic forms indicating plural S/P participants (?). 

## **Mohawk (Mithun 2022\)**

Independent pronouns, which are rarely used, distinguish singular and plural number, along with gender, only in the third person. Instead, person and number distinctions are realised through pronominal prefixes on the verb (see Figure 2). Singular, dual, and plural \[3+\] number are distinguished for first and second persons and masculine and feminine-zoic for third person agents. Only singular and plural are distinguished for masculine and feminine-zoic patients. Possessive prefixes distinguish the number of animate possessors. They are similar in form to pronominal prefixes on verbs and make the same number distinctions as their counterparts on verbs: singular/dual/plural \[3+\] for first and second persons; singular/plural for third person alienable possessors; and singular/dual/plural for inalienable third person possessors.

Figure 2\.   
![][image2]

Basic nouns are mostly neuter in gender and do not show number distinction, but distributive enclitics can be added to them that can imply number (*o-tsikhe’t-a’=shon’a* (n-sugar-ns=distr) ‘various and assorted candies’). Most of animate nominals and kinship terms are realised as verbal nouns: morphological verbs are often used as referring expressions syntactically, and they can become lexicalized as nominals, often with no further marking (*te-hni-ksa’=a*  (dv-m.DUagt-be.a.child=dim) ‘two boys’). The dual form may also occur with the duplicative prefix *te*\-, a more recent addition reinforcing duality; the plural form may contain a distributive. Though in principle distributives are not obligatory, the term for plural boys or children (though not the dual) always occurs with this distributive ending. These formations have become strongly lexicalized (*te-io-nhonhskwar-ont* (dv-fz.pat-jowl-be.attached) ‘it jowl protrudes doubly’ \= ‘cow’), and not all verbal nouns make a distinction in number, although corresponding verbs do.  
\-*anion* is used to indicate distribution over space or S/P participants (*Sa’swaht-ánion\!* ‘Turn the lights off\! (each individually)’) and can imply distribution over time or that the entities over which the action or property is distributed are various and assorted.  *\-’s* is a distributive suffix used with statives (*Raenté:ri-’s* ‘He knows each one’).   
There is a prepronominal derivational prefix, the “duplicative” *te-*, which appears in lexicalized combinations with verb roots. In a few combinations a semantic element of duality is clear (with the verb root \-*ke* ‘be multiple’ it yields a stem meaning ‘be two in number’), in other combinations an element of duality can be discerned, but somewhat less obviously, indicating a change of position or state (with the stem \-*t-a’n-* (be.standing-inchoative) it yields verbs meaning ‘stand up’).  

Summary on VDU: There is a highly lexicalized derivational ‘duplicative’ prefix without a corresponding plural form. Singular, dual, and plural \[3+\] are distinguished in pronominal prefixes on verbs and possessive prefixes on nouns (cumulatively with person and gender). Basic nouns do not distinguish number.

## **Northern Paiute (Thornes 2003\)**

Suffixes \-*mɨ* or \-*ki* mark plural on some human nouns. As the more productive expression of plurality in the language, *mɨ*\=, a proclitic to the noun phrase, functions as a plural determiner (in contrast to NOM *su*\= and OBL *ka*\= singular determiners). Both the plural suffix and the plural determiner represent the historical reduction of independent plural pronouns. Some other nouns form plural through partial reduplication (?) or irregular stem alternation.  
Sets of subject and direct object pronouns, as well as pronouns bound with postpositions, have minimal-augmented systems; 1 and 1+2 plural are formed with the suffix \-*mi*, 2 and 3 have a common plural formed with the suffix \-*mɨ*. Object proclitics and possessive proclitics have the same distinctions, but they are realized through different stems. There is also a pronominal base *na*\- which implies reciprocal or dual (‘both’).  
A number of verbs have different stems distinguishing the number of the S/P participant: 6 attested verbs (verbs of motion and position) have a three-way distinction (singular, dual, and plural, e.g. SG *winni* — DU *wammi* — PL *kono* ‘stand’) and 12 verbs have a two-way distinction (singular and plural, e.g. SG *tɨkɨ* — PL *tiuna* ‘put/place’). 3 dual stems and 1 plural \[3+\] stem are formed through partial reduplication. Langacker (1977) claims that a dual category must be a more recent development. Sometimes, both singular and plural stems of the same verb are acceptable with a plural subject (10–11).

(10)	a.	*mi=nimi	apica \-gono*  
PL= people	talk.PL \-CONT.PL  
‘Those people are talking.’ (a meeting in which there was a general discussion)  
b.	*toisu	nimmi	yadua \-gono*  
still	we.EXCL	talk.SG-CONT.PL  
‘We’re still talking.’ (context where the linguist was reviewing items of elicitation with a group)  
(11)	a.	*ma-ka		tsuga		i=gia-u*  
DEM-OBL	bisquit.root	1= give-PNC  
‘Give those roots to me\! (e.g. in a bucket)’  
b.	*ma-ka		tsuga		i=himi-u*  
DEM-OBL	bisquit.root	1= give.PL-PNC  
‘Give those roots to me\! (e.g. by the handful)’

Both verbs and nouns can show partial reduplication. With verbs, it productively encodes distributive or intraoccasional meaning (12). In some cases, partial reduplication marks the dual stem (SG *kima* — DU *kikima* — PL *kimaʔa* ‘come’).

(12)	a.	*noo-ʔyu-na		miaʔa-si	u=bu-puni-ja*  
all-NOM-ATTR	go.PL-SEQ	3-RE-see-TRNSL  
‘All of them are going to see him.’  
b.	*su=nana	u=bi-pi-ma-tatsi*  
NOM=man	3= RE-IP/butt-IP/hand-slap  
‘the man is spanking him/her’

Summary on VDU: Several verbs have different stems that distinguish singular, dual, and plural number of S/P participants. A larger number of verbs distinguishes singular and plural. Dual is argued to be a recent development. Sometimes, both singular and plural stem of the same verb is acceptable with plural S/A participants. (Pro)nominal number does not distinguish dual. Partial reduplication encodes distributive or intraoccasional meaning on verbs, and sometimes it encodes plural on nouns (?) or forms the dual stem of the verb.

## **Shoshoni (Crum 1993\)**

Personal pronouns distinguish singular, dual, and plural for first and second person (also distinguishing clusivity) in three cases (subjective, objective, possessive). Third person forms are present only for singular objective and possessive pronouns. All dual and plural pronouns have the same set of person stems. Number and case are cumulatively indicated with suffixes. Similar suffixes are used in reflexive, demonstrative, and interrogative pronouns.  
Nouns also take similar suffixes that cumulatively show number (singular, dual, and plural) and case. Sometimes, the duals and plurals are formed by reduplicating the first syllable of the noun stem, in addition to the dual and plural suffixes. In some nouns the dual and plural forms are suppletive (different stem from the singular).  
Many common verbs have different stems to indicate the number of the S/P participant. Some verbs have three stems (singular, dual, and plural), a larger number of verbs distinguish only singular and plural, and several verbs have a single stem for singular and plural, but a separate stem for dual, formed by partial reduplication (SG/PL *mi’a* — DU *mimi’a* ‘go’). Typically the dual form displays reduplication of the first syllable of either the singular or plural form, but sometimes the dual form is completely different from either the singular or the plural. A number of verbs, especially instrumental verbs, add the suffix *\-i’ih* to form the plural stem (SG *tsattamah* — PL *tsattami’ih* ‘tie’).

Summary on VDU: Some verbs have different stems that distinguish singular, dual, and plural number of S/P participants, a larger number of verbs distinguish singular and plural, and a few verbs have a single stem for singular and plural, but a separate stem for dual. Many of the dual stems are formed by partial reduplication. (Pro)nominal number also distinguishes singular, dual, and plural. 

## **Southeastern Pomo (Moshinsky 1970\)**

Personal pronouns mark plural with the suffix \-*ay*.  
The suffix \-*wi* may indicate singular on human nouns, and the suffix \-*mfo* (grammaticalized from the noun *mfo* ‘people’) may indicate plural on human nouns. There are some other irregular plural suffixes; two morphs which recur in the variants of the suffixes are \-*ay* and \-*k*. In addition, there are some irregular plural formations in human nouns derived from verbs.   
There are several verbal suffixes that indicate participant (?) plurality: \-*y*, \-*kp*, *\-mp*, \-*cp*, and \-*qp,* some of them may combine (their distribution is not entirely clear). Suffixes *\-t* and \-*w* indicate distributive (S/A/P ?) or intraoccasional plurality.   
Suffix \-*tta* may dualize one of the participants.  
Many verbs of motion and position have different stems for singular, dual, and plural \[3+\] theme (S/P ?). Mass noun participants are also indicated as plural. Some roots make only a two-way distinction, between non-plural and plural \[3+\] themes. 

Summary on VDU: Several verbal suffixes indicate participant plurality (their distribution is not entirely clear), and distributive or intraoccasional plurality may be expressed by the suffixes \-*t* and \-*w*. Suffix \-*tta* may indicate dual reference of one of the participants. Many motion and positional verbs distinguish singular, dual, and plural \[3+\] stems conditioned by the number of the theme (apparently S/P); however, some verbs make only a two-way distinction between non-plural and plural \[3+\]. Mass noun participants are also treated as plural. Personal pronouns take a plural suffix, while human nouns may take singular and plural suffixes, including several irregular plural formations. 

## **Maricopa (Gordon 1986\)**

Pronouns are unmarked for number. Most nouns are also unmarked for number; however, some human and animate nouns have optional plural forms expressed through ablaut, suffix *\-sh,* prefix *sh-/t-*, or their combination.  
Most verbs have optional dual and plural forms distinguishing the number of the subject. These forms are expressed by (combination of) different lexically distributed markers. Dual-subject stems may be derived by means of the prefixes *uu-, n-,* and *t-/sh-,* by ablaut, or by the suffixes *\-sh* and *\-v*. Plural-subject stems may be derived by means of the prefixes *uu-, a-,* and *t-/sh*\-, by ablaut, or by the suffixes *\-sh* and \-*v.* These markers partially overlap, and some are also used for nominal number; however, dual and plural forms usually differ for a given verb. There are, nevertheless, some exceptions in which the plural form is also used with dual subjects. Notably, the verbs that use morphemes restricted to either dual or plural marking (*n-* and *a-,* respectively) are all verbs of motion and position. Verbs ‘sit’, ‘stand’, ‘lie’, and ‘be located’ have suppletive dual and plural forms.  
In related languages (Diegueno, Cocopa and Yuma), the regular morphological distinction is between collective and distributive plural subjects. In Havasupai and Tolkapaya Yavapai, there is only a remnant distinction between dual and plural subjects. Collective/distributive distinction is not typically expressed in Maricopa, nor is it aligned with number distinction. However, in some speakers’ usage for a small number of forms, there seems to be a collective/distributive distinction overlapping with dual/plural distinction. In example 13, the plural form is used to emphasize distributivity.

(13)	*L.A.	'-nyvaysh-k	'e-sa	haa-k	'-nychuuvay-k*   
L.A.	1-dwell.du-ss	say-adv	different-loc	1-dwell.pl-real   
‘We (two) live in L.A. but we live in different places’. (Gordon 1986: 77\)

The prefix *nyi*\- marks plurality of the P participant. Several irregular affixes (partially overlapping with subject number affixes) are used to indicate distributivity (over place or over participants), habituality (*shmaa-m* ‘sleep’ — *shmaash-k* ‘be a sleepyhead’), or plurality of the P participant. If a verb has a separate “pluractional” stem, it is obligatorily used with a plural object (with or without the plural-object prefix *nyi*\-) even if the action was singular (14). These two stems of transitive verbs have different dual subject forms, but their plural subject stem is identical (cf. ‘hit’ in Table 3), which is not true, however, for intransitive verbs (cf. ‘be sick’). 

(14)	*nyaa	mhaa-ny-a	nyi-'-ashham-k*   
I	boy.pl-dem-Vaug	PLobj-l/3-hit.dist-real   
‘I hit the boys (with one blow)’. 

Table 3\. Verbal number forms in Maricopa

| P/A | singular subject | dual subject | plural subject |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| singular action / object | *aham-m* ‘hit’  | *ahamsh-k*  | *ashuuham-k*  |
| plural action / object | *ashham-k* ‘beat’  | *ashhamsh-k*  | *ashuuham-k*  |
| singular action / object | *'ayuu-rav-k* ‘be sick’ | *'ayuu-ravsh-k* | *'ayuu-uuraav-k* |
| plural action / object | *'ayuu-shrav-k* ‘be sickly’ | *'ayuu-shravsh-k* | *'ayuu-shuuraav-k* |

Summary on VDU: Most verbs have optional dual and plural S/A forms expressed through lexically distributed markers, including prefixes, suffixes, ablaut, and their combinations (some markers can be used for verbal dual and plural, as well as plural action/object stem and nominal plural). Dual and plural forms usually differ, although some verbs do not have a distinct dual form. Verbs with morphemes specifically associated with dual and plural marking are restricted to motion and positional verbs. In related Yuman languages, verbal number more typically distinguishes collective and distributive plural subjects, while in Maricopa only limited traces of a collective/distributive distinction overlapping with dual/plural marking remain. Plural P can be marked by the prefix *nyi*\-. In addition, some verbs obligatorily distinguish singular and plural action/object stems. For transitive verbs, these stems have different dual S/A forms, but share the same plural S/A form. Nominal number marking is limited: pronouns are unmarked for number, while only some nouns have optional plural forms.

## **Amanab (Minch 1991\)**

Personal pronouns exhibit a tripartite number system with non-cumulative number-marking: the singular is unmarked, the dual is marked by the suffix *\-ningri*, and the plural by *\-(n)ger*. However, these suffixes are reportedly rare in natural conversation and are used primarily in speech addressed to non-native speakers (see 15, where the first line reflects the spontaneous spoken form, while the second provides the corresponding careful pronunciation). Number marking on pronouns is therefore not obligatory, as subject number can generally be recovered from verbal morphology. Possessive pronouns additionally take suffix \-*na* corresponding to the genitive which is realized as \-*ni* in the plural.

(15)	*kamben minahugyi anwasafen.*  
	***ka-ger**	ambe-n	minahug-yi	anwasa-fe-n*  
	1EXCL-PL	come-RP	big road-LOC	watch-do-RP  
	‘We all came and watched (for the pig) on the big road.’

Other nominals are not marked for number (16a–b).

(16)	a.	***ruar**	ueti	tut	ne-g*  
child	little	breast	ate-PST  
‘The small child nursed.’  
b.	***ruar**	sanguari-gim	**afu-g***  
child	jungle-ALL	go.PL-PST  
‘The children went to the jungle.’

Verbs encode subject number and also exhibit a tripartite system. The singular is unmarked (17), the dual is marked by the prefix *(a)h-* (18), and the plural is realized through irregular stem alternation in intransitives (17, 16b) and vowel raising in transitives (19a–b). Vowel raising changes */e/* and */a/* to */i/* in the final syllable of the stem and on all affixes to the right.

(17)	*ka	aso-gam	**ika***  
I	garden-ALL	go  
‘I am going to the garden.’  
(18)	*Rumiau-i	Wiani-i	**ah-nimbra-n***  
Rumiau-ACC	Wiani-ACC	DU-build-RP  
‘Rumiau and Wiani both built it.’  
(19)	a.	*Moi	Timi-m	**tige-g***  
PN	PN-DA	hit-PST  
‘Moi hit Timmy.’  
b.	*Nimbre-ba	ka-na	kwai	**tigi**	ahgana-g*  
2p-TOP	1s-GEN	cassowary	hit.PL	ate-PST  
‘You all killed and ate my cassowary.’

A separate marker *fa-* is used for interoccasional plurality (20).

(20)	*ehe	skul-gam	**fe-ika-fe***  
	3	school-ALL	IT-go-do  
	‘She walks to school (every day).

Summary on VDU: Verbs may distinguish number of S/A participants: singular is unmarked, dual is marked by the prefix *(a)h-*, and plural is expressed by irregular stem alternation in intransitives and vowel raising in transitives. A separate marker *fa*\- expresses interoccasional plurality. Personal pronouns also have singular, dual, and plural forms, but number marking on pronouns is rare in natural conversation and not obligatory. Other nominals are not marked for number.

## **Imonda (Seiler 1985\)**

Kinship terms have optional dual (-*nёglel*) and plural (-*nёgal*) suffixes. For 5 human nouns, non-plural is obligatorily marked by the suffix \-*ianèi* (non-plural \< partitive \< source). The bare stem refers to the plural \[3+\]. However, the non-plural suffix is absent if there is a numeral that precedes the noun. Other nouns, as well as personal pronouns, do not show number distinction.  
Most verbs have a tripartite distinction, with singular being unmarked.  
Prefix *e(h)*\- is used for dual human subjects (21), while the suffix \-*ual* is used if the subject or the object is dual (22), and it may combine with *e(h)*\-. Since \-*ual* may refer to both A and P, in ambiguous cases, \-*ual* is used for P and *e(h)-* for A (23). \-*ual* also appears as an integral part of a number of transitive verb stems that denote events that result in the halving of the object (‘break’ with different types of objects; 24). 5 stems are attested that change medial \-*d*\- or \-*h*\- to \-*th*\- for dual objects.

(21)	*tëh-fa		e-i-ab-hô-puhô		fe-n*  
firewood-TO	DL-CL-PL-put-come.up	do-PST  
‘They stacked up the firewood.’   
(22)	*sue	ta-ual-f*  
fire	burn-DL-PRS  
‘There are two fires burning.’   
(23)	a.	*ièf	mugasl		ka	e-nibia-f*  
house	one		1	DL-build-PRS  
‘We two build one house.’   
b.	*ièf	sabla	nibia-ual-f*  
house	two	build-DL-PRS  
‘I build two houses.’   
(24)	*atha		toual-u*  
sugarcane	break-IMP  
‘Break the sugarcane\!’ 

There are several ways of marking plural. 

* Collective subject plural is often unmarked (25).

(25)	*id	kubui	isi-ia-m		föhô-n*  
men	INT	hunt.pigs-LOC-GL	go.down-PST  
‘Lots of men went pig hunting.’ 

* Subject plural is most commonly marked through raising of the last vowel.   
* Several verbs (‘eat’, ‘stand’, ‘not like’, ‘make netbag’, ‘sleep’, ‘lie’) have suppletive forms for plural subjects.   
* Verbs of motion mark plural with the prefix *ai-* if the prefix slot is not occupied by another motion verb marker. With uncountable participants, *ai-* indicates a great quantity.   
* Plural subject marker \-*fia* is used if the verb stem is followed by *\-ula*, as well as for several other verbs.  
* The verb stems *pia* ‘come’ and *uagl* ‘go’ occurring in serialisation after the lexical verb stem may be used to mark subject plural.  
* Suffix \-*uo͂l,* which triggers the pro-verb *fe* ‘make, do’, is used for some intransitive verbs to indicate plural S-participant (‘vomit’, ‘cough’, ‘be’, etc.), but it is more common for plural P-participants. With uncountable P, *\-uo͂l* indicates a great quantity. Moreover, \-*uo͂l* may be used to indicate intensive and habitual.  
* Verbs ‘cut’ and ‘see’ have idiosyncratic object plural forms.

Several verbs distinguish only singular and plural objects. Verbs ‘follow’ and ‘hear’ have idiosyncratic plural forms. Prefix \-*abu* marks the plural P or BEN for a number of verbs that end in *\-(f)ia* or are polymorphemic consisting of an adjunct plus the proverb *fe* ‘make, do’. However, most of these verbs have alternative ways of marking dual or plural objects.  
The number of IOs is also distinguished. The verb ‘give’ marks the singular recipient with \-*h*, while the plural is unmarked. Singular beneficiary is marked with \-*na*, plural is marked with \-*n*. These markers are optional for some types of beneficiaries of some verbs. The same markers may also optionally encode human possessor number.  
Some verbs take classifiers that may also change for number.

Summary on VDU: Most verbs have a tripartite number distinction, with singular unmarked. Dual human S/A participants are marked by the prefix *e(h)-,* while the suffix \-*ual* may encode dual S/A/P participants and may combine with *e(h)*\-. In ambiguous cases, \-*ual* is used for P and *e(h)-* for A. The suffix \-*ual* also occurs as an integral part of some transitive verb stems denoting events that result in the halving of P. Some stems mark dual P by consonant changes. Plural marking has many strategies, including final-vowel raising, stem alternation for S/A/P participant number, the motion-verb prefix *ai*\-, the plural S/A marker \-*fia*, the suffix \-*uo͂l* for plural S/P, the prefix *abu*\- for plural P or BEN. Collective S/A plural is often unmarked. Although many verbs distinguish both dual and plural, the paradigmatic relation of these forms is questionable. Outside the verbal domain, kinship terms may take optional dual and plural suffixes, five human nouns obligatorily mark non-plural, and other nouns and personal pronouns do not show number distinction.

## **Waris (Brown 1990\)**

There is no pronominal number. Human nouns (a small class) have an unmarked plural form; singular is marked with \-*rini* (= ablative case) and dual with \-*rini-sambla* (*sambla* ‘two’).   
Plural \[3+\] subject is marked by vowel raising, suppletion, or prefix *a*\-. Dual subject is marked by prefix *e-* or reduplication of stem-initial vowel. The meaning of dual subject prefix *e-* may also be expanded to apply to two groups of people (26).

(26)	*kembelnind	hi-mba		hev-m		e-wal-wol		e-ve-vna*  
village.people	3rd-TOP	3rd.EMP-GL	DL-shoot-NS.O	DL-do-CON  
‘People (from two clans) were shooting arrows at one another.’

Verbs of motion, sitting and standing can be prefixed for the number of things being held or carried at the same time (27): *wul*\- (singular), *hai*\- (dual), *i*\- (plural \[3+\]).

(27)	*ti	hai-e-nga-v*  
wood	two.carried-DL.S-go-PRS  
‘Two are each carrying a piece of wood.’

Most verbs of action can be prefixed to indicate the number of people one is accompanying (28): *wai*\- (singular), *won*\- (plural).

(28)	*indhana-m-ba	wóh-va	ka-va	won-i-pró-na*  
people-GL-TOP	cargo-TOP	1st-TOP	PLACC-PLheld-come-PST  
‘I came bringing people and cargo.’

Plural (distributive?) P may be marked by the suffix \-*wol* or by a separate stem. For many verbs there is no distinction between dual and plural P, but for the stem *ve* ‘do’, there is a full paradigm for singular, dual, and plural S and P. The suffix \-*wol* can also indicate intraoccasional plurality (29), distribution in space or time (of S?), and frequentative (? ‘do sth a lot’), it can be affixed to verbs of motion as well. In example (30), the stem is prefixed to agree in number with the dual S and suffixed with \-*wol*, which indicates that the death of the father and the death of the mother were different events. If the stem becomes long, an auxiliary verb is used to carry number and tense information.

(29)	*ka-va		hélve-na / hélvo-wol	ve-na*  
1st-TOP	hit-PST / hit-NS.O	do-PST  
‘I hit (it) once / many times.’  
(30)	*araraval-va	ka-na-m-ba	doara	e-ndaha-wol-mana-na*  
fa.mo.-TOP 	1st-GEN-GL-TOP	previously	DL.S-die-NS.O-BEN.SG-PST  
‘My father and mother died already (at different times).’

Verbs can also indicate benefactive and recipient number: \-*mana* (benefactive singular), \-*in* (benefactive plural), \-*ho* (recipient singular), \-*hun* (recipient plural). Subject number is neutralized when the plural benefactee is suffixed to some verb stems.

Summary on VDU: Dual S/A is marked by prefix *e-* or reduplication of stem-initial vowel, a corresponding plural \[3+\] form may be marked by vowel raising, stem alternation, or prefix *a*\-. Dual may also apply to two groups of people. Suffix \-*wol* or stem alternation mark plural (distributive?) S/P, as well as intraoccasional plurality and frequentative (?). Verbs of motion, sitting and standing can be prefixed for the number of things being held or carried (singular, dual, plural \[3+\]), and verbs of action may be prefixed for the number of people accompanying (singular, plural). Benefactive and recipient number does not distinguish dual. Human nouns (a small class) have an unmarked plural form; singular and dual is marked.

## **Kilmeri (Gerstner-Link 2018\)**

Personal pronouns distinguish singular, dual, and plural (as well as three persons and clusivity). Dual is derived from singular by means of the suffix \-*yo* (= LOC). The inclusive dual consists of three elements: second person singular, inclusive plural, and locative \-*yo*. Plural forms are not systematically related to singular. The actual use of pronouns tends to substitute the inclusive dual with the inclusive plural, and so there is a usage-based syncretism of dual and plural. Possessive pronouns are derived from personal pronouns.   
Dual S/A is obligatorily marked on the verb by *i-/-i.* Several intransitive verbs (6 verbs referring to uncontrolled states) take dual suffix \-*we* instead, which is usually used with transitive verbs as an obligatory dual P marker. Dual marking is also used when the action results in two pieces of the participant (e.g., ‘cut in two pieces’). There are rare cases when singular or plural is used instead of the dual form. Dual A and dual P marking may combine, but in example (31), only dual A is indicated, because each dug one hole (in contrast to Waris and Madi).

(31)	*dedukoyo	bî	dupua	raro-i*    
	we.DUINCL	hole	two	dig.PP-DUA   
‘The two of us dug two holes.’ \> Each of us dug one hole. \[IV,131\] 

In most verbs the plural is not marked morphologically and shows the same form as the singular. But a number of verbs employ a separate plural \[3+\] stem. The plural \[3+\] forms tend to vanish in the speech of less fluent speakers which is indicative of the fact that the meaning of the verb is conceptually tied to the singular. 19 intransitive and 34 transitive alternating verbs are attested. Two intransitive verbs use these forms also for the dual. Many of the transitive verbs employ reduplication, among other means, to form their plural stem. Participants may also be uncountable. 6 verbs have a distinct stem for plural A participant.  
A relatively productive suffix \-*wepi* (54 verbs attested) indicates multiple S/P participants; it may be used with uncountable participants as well. In some contexts it has an intensifying function and is also argued to indicate event plurality (?), and sometimes has an idiosyncratic meaning. Only six verbs out of the 53 singular-plural pairs are also found suffixed by \-*wepi*. Both irregular plural stems and \-*wepi* may have referential capacity.  
If there is a free pronoun, there has to be an obligatory match between pronominal and verbal number. Sometimes, singular is used with plural reference although the verb may have a plural stem (32). The correlation of verbal number and nominal reference is illustrated in Table 4\.

(32)	*bi	sele-yo	sele-yo	uke	wok	ar	pi	bi	wip	ni*   
pig	garden-LOC	come.hither	we.EXCL	work NEG	LV	pig	taro	eat  
‘The pigs come to the gardens, (when) we don’t work there, the pigs feed on taro \[and ruin the crop\].’ 

Table 4\. Correlation of vernal number and nominal reference  
![][image3]  
Suffix \-*mapi* is not commonly attested, but it may indicate intraoccasional or interoccasional plurality. Prefix *wo*\- indicates collective (or accompanied?) plural S/A. Suffix \-*ini* encodes plural recipient.

Summary on VDU: Dual S/A is obligatorily marked on the verb by *i-/-i*, while a small class of intransitive verbs instead takes the dual suffix \-*we*, otherwise used as an obligatory dual P marker on transitive verbs (dual A and dual P marking may combine, but not readily). Dual marking may also indicate that an action results in two pieces of a participant. Dual forms are not paradigmatically matched to plural ones. Many verbs do not morphologically distinguish singular and plural, but a number of verbs (53 verbs) have distinct plural \[3+\] S/P stems (two of them use these forms for dual as well). A relatively productive suffix \-*wepi* marks multiple S/P participants and may additionally express intensification, event plurality (?), or idiosyncratic meanings. Plural stems and \-*wepi* may both have referential capacity. Singular forms may occasionally be used with plural reference despite the existence of plural stems. Additional markers include suffix \-*mapi* for temporal plurality, prefix *wo*\- for collective/accompanied plural S/A, and suffix \-*ini* for plural recipients. Personal pronouns distinguish singular, dual, and plural number, although the inclusive dual is frequently replaced in usage by the inclusive plural. 

## **Northeast Kiwai (Schulz & Petterson 2022\)**

Not all nouns indicate number, but some nouns express plural with a separate stem, and some other nouns attach the suffix \-*oi* or \-*bai’oi*. Distributive meaning may be expressed by reduplication. The dual suffix *\-ti \~ \-oti* (described as a quantifier) can be added to any noun to express two specimens of the referent: (*pee-ti* ‘two canoes’).  
Pronouns distinguish first, second and third person, and singular, dual, trial and plural number. The dual and trial are formed by the addition of the dual suffix \-*ti* or the trial suffix \-*bi* to the plural pronoun. The dual pronouns are commonly used, but the trial pronoun is less commonly used, with speakers defaulting to the plural.  
Subject number (S/A) on verbs distinguishes singular, dual, trial (cannot be used with four referents), and plural \[2+\], but many people use the plural \[2+\] form for dual and trial as well. It is possible to use either the dual or trial pronoun, with plural \[2+\] marking on the verb (33). Singular is overtly marked only in the first and second person of the intermediate past by the suffix \-*die*. Dual is marked by the suffix *\-ido/-udo*, plural \[2+\] by \-*umo*, and trial by \-*bii* (the same suffix that is used with pronouns), which cooccurs with plural \[2+\] marking. 

(33)	a.	*Rii-bii		oti-bii-ka-umo.*  
3PL-TRI	stand-TRI-PRS-PLSBJ  
‘They-3 stand.’  
b.	*Rii-bii		oti-ka-umo.*  
3PL-TRI	stand-PRS-PLSBJ  
‘They-3 stand.’

Plural object is marked by the prefix *i-,* which is also used for plural beneficiary and plural middle voice (however, they are argued to be other homophonous prefixes). Ray (1933:46) describes dual and trial object marking in Southern Kiwai, but these do not exist in Northeast Kiwai. At least two verbs (‘cook’, ‘build’) have unique forms to express singular and plural objects.  
Verbal suffix \-*uti* marks distributive plurality of P (but may also cooccur with the habitual suffix), and suffix \-*tuti* marks distributive plurality of S/A/P and continuative (? ‘keep doing sth’).

Summary on VDU: Verbs distinguish singular, dual, trial, and plural \[2+\] S/A participants; however, plural \[2+\] forms are frequently used instead of dual and trial. Dual is marked by the suffix *\-ido/-udo*, plural by *\-umo*, and trial by \-*bii* cooccurring with plural \[2+\] marking. Plural P is marked by the prefix *i-*, while dual and trial P marking reported for Southern Kiwai is absent in Northeast Kiwai. Some verbs have suppletive forms for plural P. Verbal suffixes \-*uti* (P) and \-*tuti* (S/A/P) express distributive plurality and may additionally convey habitual or continuative meanings.  Dual and trial pronominal forms are derived from plural forms by suffixation. Some nouns take plural suffix or indicate plural with another stem, they also may attach dual suffix (described as a quantifier).

## **Amele (Roberts 2016\)**

Personal pronouns distinguish singular, dual, and plural number through person-number stems, with syncretism between second and third person in dual and plural forms. Verbs index S/A and P participants separately by means of suffixes exhibiting the same distinctions and syncretic patterns. Inalienable possessive suffixes follow the same morphology, while kinship terms additionally mark plural possessum with the suffix *\-el/-il/-ul*.  
The language distinguishes a singular specific determiner (*oso*) and a plural specific determiner (*leih*), which may function either attributively within the referential phrase or pronominally. Some interrogative pronouns also distinguish singular and plural forms, the latter marked by the prefix *a*\-.  
Nouns may be reduplicated to express various lexically conditioned meanings, including plurality, similarity, emphasis, reciprocity, and distributive reference.  
Markers formally identical to the second/third person dual suffix \-*al* and plural suffix \-*ad* (34-35) may additionally express event quantification and may correspond to distributive or intraoccasional plurality (there are no examples of the latter, and no examples of first person with these suffixes). The suffix \-*ad* may also express an “exclusive action” meaning.

(34)	a.	*Caja		age	bud-u		bel-ad-ein.*   
woman		3pl	disperse-DV	go.nsg-DSTR.pl-3PLNOM.RMP  
‘The women dispersed in all directions / each went to her own place.’   
b.	*Dana	ale	cal-al-esin.*  
man	3du	arrive-DSTR.du-3DUNOM.RMP  
‘The men both arrived.’  
(35)	*ija cu\~cul-h-i l-im-ig nu-ad-ig-a=da.*  
1sg DUR\~leave-2SGACC-DV go-SS.SEQ-1SGNOM go-EXCL-1SGNOM-TP=ASS  
‘So I had to leave and go without you.’

Reduplicated nominal spatial postposition \=*nana* has meaning ‘in every location’ or ‘towards every goal’.   
Rightward reduplication (or, in some cases, irregular stem alternation) of the verbal stem expresses iterative meaning, i.e. intra- or interoccasional plurality (?). 

Summary on VDU: Verbs index singular, dual, and plural S/A and P participants by means of person-number suffixes. Markers formally identical to dual and plural second/third person suffixes (*\-al, \-ad*) are reported to express distributive or intraoccasional duality/plurality (?), while \-*ad* may also convey an “exclusive action” meaning. Personal pronouns and inalienable possessive suffixes employ the same system as verbal indexing, while kinship terms additionally mark plurality of the possessed referent. Additionally, intra- or interoccasional plurality may be expressed by rightward verbal reduplication or irregular stem alternation, nominal reduplication may also indicate lexically conditioned meanings.

## **Suki (Tongeren 2022\)**

Pronouns distinguish singular and plural number cumulatively with person and case.   
Several human nouns are obligatory reduplicated to indicate plural number, some other nouns may be reduplicated to indicate ‘lots of…’ or an idiosyncratic meaning. Several adjectives (8 attested) have a dedicated plural form.   
The specificity marker distinguishes singular (*\=ti*) and plural (*\=diti / \=der*), and it can occur on demonstratives, interrogatives, adjectives, nouns, and noun phrases.  
The associative plural marker \=*di* is used on personal names and kin terms to extend their reference to include the person’s associates; it is also required on kin terms with non-singular reference. NP enclitic \=*yege* is an infrequent marker of plurality (although it may not be the only meaning), which appears more frequent on non-human, modified, and non-verbal predicate NPs.  
Direct and indirect object suffixes distinguish singular and plural cumulative with person, but they do not differentiate second and third person. The first person singular DO  marker \-*ne* is formally identical to the first person singular subject pronoun, and the second/third person non-singular DO marker \-*de* matches the second person non-singular subject pronoun. The second/third singular DO marker is zero, but a select set of highly transitive verbs take \-*ma* for this value instead, a form borrowed from the IO set.  
Some verbs optionally (?) mark plural S/P by *im/um* (8 intransitive verbs). Another group of verbs (they are mostly transitive and generally have a telic/punctual Aktionsart and cut/break semantics; 14 verbs) has a repetition of the right-most oral stop of their singular root. There are also some verbs (5 verbs) which have repeated stops in their roots throughout, regardless of participant number, e.g. ‘knock’ and ‘shake’. The posture verbs (3 verbs) apply the same strategy to form “iterative” roots (intra- or interoccasional plurality), however, some of them also have alternation for the number of the subject, so that one verb may have four stems. 10 other verbs form plural by other alternations (reduplication of more than one stop alone, truncation, and replacement of r by t).  
Verbs ‘come’, ‘go’, and ‘move around’ distinguish singular, dual, and plural \[3+\] stems. The motion verbs are the only verbs whose number-differentiated roots are not formally related to each other.  
Subject number suffixes distinguish number (singular and plural) and person (and also have two sets, for past and non-past), but second and third person are not differentiated in the singular. A dual subject marker \-*dr* (in slot 3\) is frequent, but not obligatory, it provides further specification of the plural number value. Middle verbs take a middle marker \-*se* (in slot 1\) when the subject is plural; and intransitive verbs take the inanimate marker \-*tat* (in slot 3\) when the subject is plural and inanimate.  
Serial verb constructions are marked for pluractionality, i.e. whether SVC or V1 represents a repeated situation (by the same participant or by different participants). Pluractionality is also distinguished in similative constructions.

Summary on VDU: Verbs ‘come’, ‘go’, and ‘move around’ distinguish singular, dual, and plural \[3+\] stems. Some other verbs optionally mark plural S/P by the suffixes \-*im/-um*. Stop repetition may denote S/P plural or intra- or interoccasional plurality for posture verbs (which have separate plural stems). Sets of subject, direct object and indirect object suffixes distinguish singular and plural cumulative with person. Subject dual (S/A) marker \-*dr* optionally specifies dual reference (and does not have a corresponding plural form). Middle and intransitive verbs can take a plural suffix (-*se* or \-*tat*). Pluractionality is marked in serial verb constructions and similative. Pronouns distinguish singular and plural, while some nouns, adjectives, demonstratives, interrogatives, and noun phrases may take plural markers. 

## **Culina (Dienst 2014\)**

Suffix (or postposition?) \-*deni* can be used to express plural with common human nouns and personal pronouns or associative plural with proper human nouns, usually (but not necessarily) for second and third person (the distinction between first person singular and plural is described as one of person rather than number).   
Some verbs are inflecting, and some inflect with the help of auxiliary. Verbal suffix \-*mana* can (optionally?) indicate plural S/A. On the auxiliary, plural is also marked by \-*mana* or, in certain contexts, by *ke*\- (+ \-*ra*).  
Suffix \-*bakhi* marks plural number of direct and indirect objects (and can thus be ambiguous when there are both a countable direct object and a countable indirect object); it is also attested as a subject plural marker on two intransitive verbs (‘be born’, ‘disperse’). The prefix *ta*\- indicates plural \[3+\] direct object. The dual of the direct object can be expressed through the reduplication of the final syllable of the verb stem if the latter has at least two syllables, otherwise, object dual is indicated by the triplication of the stem vowel. The prefix *ta*\- and partial stem reduplication thus have complementary functions.
