A number of verbs (‘run’, ‘move’, ‘lie on the ground’, ‘fall’, ‘be born’, ‘stand’, ‘sleep’, ‘sit on the ground’, ‘die’, ‘hang up’, ‘kill’, ‘put’, ‘take’) have different stems to express number of the S/P participant. Only some have a dual form, the others use either the singular or the plural \[2+\] stem or both for dual as well.   
Plural S of stative verbs with an auxiliary is marked by \-*khiri* on the main verb (in the second person plural, the plural number is also marked by the prefix *ke*\- on the auxiliary). Dual is marked by reduplication of the last syllable of the main verb, the auxiliary has the same form as the plural in the first person and as the singular in the second and third person.

Summary on VDU: A number of verbs distinguish the number of the S/P participant through stem alternation; however, only some of them have distinct dual forms, while others use singular and/or plural \[2+\] stems for dual as well. Dual P (as well as stative S) may be expressed through partial stem reduplication, while plural \[3+\] P is marked by the prefix *ta*\-. In stative constructions with auxiliaries, plural S is marked by \-*khiri* on the main verb, while dual is expressed through reduplication of the final syllable of the main verb (the auxiliary shows mixed agreement patterns: in dual constructions it has the same form as plural in the first person, but the same form as singular in the second and third person). Some verbs do not distinguish dual and mark only plural (-*bakhi* for P/IO, \-*mana* for S/A). Personal pronouns and nouns may distinguish singular and plural but not dual. 

## **Madi (Dixon 2004\)**

There are several similar sets of personal pronouns: object pronouns, subject pronouns, cardinal pronouns, alienable and inalienable possessive pronouns, they have person-number stems distinguishing singular and plural (as well as three persons, clusivity and, sometimes, animacy in the third person). The pronouns are free phonological forms (apart from first and second person singular object), but they are obligatorily used even if the argument is expressed by an NP.   
About 10 stance verbs have different stems for singular, dual, and plural \[3+\] S/P participants. There is some neutralization between semantically related verbs in dual and plural \[3+\] (cf. Table 5). The verb ‘be hanging from a hook, lie in a hammock’ has a common stem for singular and plural, but a different stem for dual S.   
Table 5\. Verbs of lying in Madi

| meaning | SG | DU | PL\[3+\] |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| ‘lie on ground’ | *\-homa-* |  *mata \-na-*  |  *soo (to-)na(-sa)*  |
| ‘lie on raised surface’  | *\-forl-* |  |  |
| ‘lie in water’ | *hofa- \~ \-fowa-* |  |  |

About 9 further verbs have two different stems distinguishing singular and plural S/P participants, for dual reference either the singular or the plural root is used, plus dual suffix *\-ikima*.   
Verbal suffix *\-ikima* indicates that one of the arguments (S/P, or, sometimes some other constituent) involves two (a pair of) people or things or places. A transitive clause with \-*ikima* may refer to two A participants and two P participants, each A relating to one P (36). One consultant gave \-*ikima* as the dual correspondent of distributive \-*ri* for ‘respectively’.

(36)	*karaboha	mee		tiwa			ka-ni.kima*   
blow.gun(F)	3NSGA	carry.on.shoulder	APPLIC-AUXA.TWOf  
‘The two of them each carries a blowgun on his shoulder.’

The second order prefix *ka*\- with some verbs has a syntactic effect, deriving a transitive stem from an intransitive root, while with other verbs it does not affect transitivity but indicates one of a number of semantic modifications. The most common semantic sense of *ka*\- is to indicate that an animate S or P argument (although there are examples with inanimate objects) has dual reference (37). The prefix *ka*\- may also be used to denote not two people but instead two groups of people. *ka*\- is argued to differ from \-*ikima* in terms of animacy, meaning (‘two’ rather than ‘pair’) and participants involved (-*ikima* often refers to a pair of A and a pair of P, each A with one P). A small class of verbs take the prefix *ka*\- in another sense, to indicate that the S/P argument has singular reference; when *ka*\- is omitted the S/P is understood to refer to ‘many entities’ (e.g., *tao ka-na-* ‘shoot (one animal)’, *tao \-na-* ‘shoot (many animals)’). For a further very small class of verbs *ka*\- has the opposite effect: when *ka*\- is present, there are multiple referents and when *ka*\- is omitted there is a single referent (e.g. *tani \-na-* ‘(one thing) slides’, *tani ka-na* ‘(several things) slide’). 

(37)	*Jaras mee joo ki-ne-ke.*  
Branco(M) 3NSGS wade APPLIC-CONTf-DECf  
‘Two Brancos are wading in the water.’  

Verbal suffix \-*rawa* is used when any of the core participants (S/A/P) — or, very occasionally, a peripheral participant — is feminine and has plural reference.

Summary on VDU: About 10 stance verbs have distinct singular, dual, and plural \[3+\] stems conditioned by the number of the S/P participant; there is some neutralization between semantically related verbs in the dual and plural \[3+\]. One verb has a shared singular/plural stem but a distinct dual stem. Another group of verbs distinguishes only singular and plural stems and uses the dual suffix *\-ikima* for dual reference (with either a singular or a plural stem). Suffix \-*ikima* may indicate dual reference of S/P or other constituents; it is argued to apply to pairs rather than simply to two participants, and in transitive clauses it typically combines with distributive action. The applicative *ka*\- often indicates dual reference of animate S/P participants, though for some verbs it instead marks singular or plural reference. The prefix may also refer to two groups rather than two individuals. Verbal suffix \-*rawa* marks feminine plural reference of core participants. Personal pronouns distinguish singular and plural, but not dual. 

## **Xerénte (Filho 2007\)**

Nouns and pronouns may optionally attach the pluralizing suffix \-*nõri͂* (which is argued to be a derivational formative rather than inflectional). It is usually used when the verb does not differentiate number.  
Some verbs have separate stems for dual and plural S/P participants.

Summary on VDU: Some verbs have separate stems for dual and plural S/P participants. Number can be marked on nouns or pronouns by a pluralizing suffix (especially if it is not marked on the verb).

## **Shipibo-Conibo (Valenzuela 2003\)**

(Absolutive) personal pronouns have person-number stems distinguishing singular and plural number. Ergative, possessive modifier, possessive, interessive, and other forms are derived from these stems by affixation.  
Countable nouns may attach the suffix \-*bo* to express plural meaning (38), which is optional if number is marked on the verb. Names of ethnic groups are also usually marked with \-*bo* (cf. Shipi-bo ‘the Tamarin Monkey People’, Koni-bo ‘the Eel People’). \-*bo* is also used to form the third person plural pronoun *ja-bo*, and sometimes is attached to other pronouns. It attaches to the last word of the corresponding noun phrase, even if it is not the head (but it may also be present on a second element inside the NP). Besides encoding plurality of individuals, \-*bo* can indicate plurality of kinds (e.g., different kinds of people).

(38)	*Isa-(bo)-ra		noya-(kan)-ai.*  
bird-(PL:ABS)-EV	fly-(PL)-INC  
‘The birds are flying.’ 

Verbal suffix \-*kan* indicates plural S/A participant. It is optional in numeral constructions or if number is marked on the subject.  
Verbs ‘come’ and ‘go’ have separate stems for their plural or transitive (causative) counterpart (*jo*\- ‘come (SG)’, *ka*\- ‘go (SG)’, *be*\- ‘come (PL), bring’ *bo*\- ‘go (PL), carry’). *be*\- and *bo*\- are used for subjects such as ‘rain,’ ‘flooding,’ ‘clouds,’ ‘school of fish,’ ‘wind,’ ‘waves,’ etc. (uncountable nouns in meteorological constructions), as well as for plural subjects. Co-expression of plural and transitive is also present in ventive (-*kiran* vs \-*beiran*) and andative (-*kain* vs \-*bain*) suffixes, which might have arisen through grammaticalization of forms involving the motion verb roots.   
Suffix \-*bekon* can indicate that the action is carried out by two participants. For verbs ‘come’ and ‘go’, the singular stem is used with this suffix, so the author argues, that it rather signals a single participant accompanied by a second one (which would be compatible with its probable etymology: \-*be* comitative \+ \-*kon* ‘true, core, legitimate’). It is also used when a reciprocal action involves two participants. In example 39, \-*bekon* combines with the plural suffix.

(39)	*Ja-ska-raino-a-xonki	ino	betan*	  
that-SIML-ra:LOC:LOC-ABL-S:HSY	jaguar	and   
*xae-ki	rawi-Arnnan-bekon-a	iki.*   
anteater:ABS-HSY2	(become)enemy-PL:REC-DUAL-PP2	AUX   
‘Since this time, the jaguar and the anteater are enemies.’ 

Reduplication takes place with verbal, adjectival, adjunct, and nominal stems, the meanings associated with reduplication are described as iterative or continuous action, intensification, emphasis, plurality, and distribution. There is also a suffix \-*pake* ‘one by one’ (derived from the verb ‘cause to fall’) which can express distributive action.

Summary on VDU: Verbal suffix \-*kan* optionally marks plural S/A participants, while the motion verbs ‘come’ and ‘go’ have distinct singular and plural stems, the latter also being used with certain uncountable subjects and in transitive contexts. Suffix \-*bekon* indicates that an action is carried out by two participants; with ‘come’ and ‘go’, however, it combines with singular stems, though it may also cooccur with the plural suffix \-*kan*. It is also used with reciprocal actions involving two participants. Additionally, reduplication has a wide range of functions, and there is also a verbal distributive suffix. Nouns optionally distinguish singular and plural, while pronouns distinguish person and singular/plural number.
